proof:
# Proper cap partitions have at most two caps per midpoint component
fiber families. It is not an inequality for arbitrary overlapping small
cap covers, and it does not complete OC. Its restrictive partition and
no-whole-fiber premises are explicit throughout.

## 1. Statement

Let C be a convex body in R^n times R^d and S its nonempty mixed-integer
intersection. Let q=dim_H(S)>=1 and let mu=H_q restricted to S. Let P
be the finite set of bases whose fibers K_z have affine dimension q.
Write V_z=H_q(K_z)>0 and M=sum_{z in P}V_z. Lower-dimensional integer
fibers carry zero mu-mass. Let k be the number of occupied parities of P.

Join each same-parity pair z,w in P and its integer midpoint h=(z+w)/2
in one hyperedge. The midpoint belongs to P, as proved below. Let c(P)
be the number of connected components of this finite hypergraph.

Consider r closed ambient halfspaces H_1,...,H_r with positive masses
mu(H_i)>0. Assume:

1. their traces cover mu-almost all S;
2. mu(H_i intersect H_j)=0 for every i!=j;
3. H_q(K_z intersect H_i)<V_z for every z in P and every i.

Thus the cap traces form a partition up to null overlaps, and no cap
captures a whole positive fiber, even in measure. Then

    r<=2c(P)<=2k.                                      (1)

For every z in P exactly two cap traces have positive fiber measure;
they are complementary cuts on its affine span. Their unordered pair
of global cap indices is constant on each midpoint component.

Moreover c(P)=k implies |P|=k. In particular, if |P|>k then

    r<=2(k-1).                                        (2)

If all actual global cap masses equal a common D>0, disjointness and
coverage give M=rD, and consequently

    D>=M/[2c(P)]>=M/(2k).                             (3)

For q>=1, Gamma_q<=1/2, so this is at least Gamma_q M/k. It is a
numerical obstruction to a small equal-budget cap PARTITION under
the three premises, not to an arbitrary small cap cover.

## 2. A single convex body cannot be partitioned into three proper caps

**Lemma.** Let K be a full-dimensional compact convex body in a real
affine space of positive dimension. A finite closed-halfspace cover
of K, with pairwise zero-volume overlaps and all positive traces proper,
has exactly two positive traces. Their boundary hyperplanes coincide,
and their orientations are opposite.

**Proof.** An almost-everywhere cover by finitely many closed sets is
already a cover of K: a point outside the union has a relatively open
neighborhood disjoint from it, whose intersection with the interior of
K has positive volume. A trace of zero volume misses int(K), unless
it contains the full affine space, in which case it has positive volume.

Choose any positive proper cap H_i. Its hyperplane L_i cuts int(K).
At p in L_i intersect int(K), no other cap can contain p strictly:
an open half-neighborhood on the H_i side would then have positive
overlap. Thus all other cap margins at p are nonpositive. Choose
points in int(K) strictly on the opposite side of L_i approaching p.
They are covered by other caps. Finiteness and closedness show that
p lies on the boundary of at least one other cap. Consequently

    L_i intersect int(K) subset union_{j!=i} L_j.

In dimension at least two, a finite union of proper lower-dimensional
affine subspaces cannot cover the relatively open set on the left.
Hence some L_j equals L_i. In dimension one the hyperplanes are
singletons, and the same conclusion is immediate. Coincident
orientations would give a positive overlap, so this cap's orientation
is opposite. Its trace has positive volume, since L_i cuts int(K).
The two caps cover the entire affine space. Any third positive cap
would therefore overlap at least one of them in positive volume,
contradicting the premise. QED.

This lemma also shows why the no-whole-fiber assumption matters. With
that assumption removed, a fiber can instead have a single full cap,
and need not have an interior common cutting point of two caps.

## 3. The actual midpoint inclusion preserves the pair label

Apply the lemma in the intrinsic affine q-plane of each K_z. Assumption
3 excludes the full-cap alternative; the fiber must therefore have two
positive traces with one common cutting hyperplane and opposite
intrinsic normals. Let I_z be this unordered pair of cap indices.
Choose x_z in the relative interior of their common section. Since
that hyperplane cuts the relative interior of K_z, x_z belongs to
relint(K_z). Both margins indexed by I_z are zero at (z,x_z).

Every other cap has zero q-volume on K_z and hence has strictly
negative margin at (z,x_z). To justify strictness, if its intrinsic
normal is nonzero, a zero margin through a relative interior point
would cut positive volume. If its intrinsic normal vanishes, a zero
margin includes the entire fiber, again contradicting zero volume.

Now let z,w in P have the same parity and let h=(z+w)/2. Convexity
gives

    (K_z+K_w)/2 subset K_h.

The direction space of the affine hull of the Minkowski sum is the
sum of the two q-dimensional direction spaces. Since K_h is an
integer fiber and no such fiber has dimension greater than q, those
spaces must agree. The midpoint fiber therefore has dimension q as
well, belongs to P, and has that same direction space.

The point x_h^*=(x_z+x_w)/2 is in relint(K_h): intrinsic balls about
x_z and x_w give an intrinsic ball about their midpoint in the
Minkowski sum. Every cap margin is affine in the full ambient point.
At (h,x_h^*), its margin is zero precisely for the indices in
I_z intersect I_w, and is strictly negative for all other indices.

If that intersection were empty, the midpoint would be uncovered,
contradicting the fiber cover. If it had one element i, all other
caps would remain strictly absent on a small intrinsic neighborhood
of the midpoint. The intrinsic normal of H_i is nonzero on the common
q-direction space, since H_i is a proper positive cut at both source
fibers. An open half-neighborhood of the midpoint on the negative
side of H_i would then be uncovered, a positive-volume contradiction.
Thus the intersection has two elements, and I_z=I_w.

Those two caps also both cut an open part of K_h at their common
midpoint. They therefore have positive q-volume there. The one-fiber
lemma forces I_h=I_z=I_w. This proves constancy along each midpoint
hyperedge, and hence along each midpoint component.

All reasoning occurs in actual integer fibers with their intrinsic
volumes. No replacement of their union by conv(S), arbitrary affine
lattice transformation, or unproved closure of an individual midpoint
component is used.

## 4. The cap count and the occupied-parity count

Every positive global cap has a positive trace on at least one fiber,
because mu is the finite sum of the positive intrinsic fiber measures.
It therefore occurs in some pair I_z. Each of the c(P) components
supplies a single pair, so their union contains at most 2c(P) indices.
This proves the first inequality in (1). Distinct components can use
overlapping pairs, which only reduces the number of distinct caps.

All points of a fixed parity belong to the same component, since any
two form a hyperedge with their midpoint. The map from the k occupied
parities onto the c(P) components is surjective; hence c(P)<=k.

If c(P)=k, that map is bijective. Every component then consists of one
parity class, and the midpoint of any two of its points belongs to
the same component and hence the same parity. A finite set of one
parity closed under pairwise midpoints has only one point: a closest
distinct pair would have a distinct midpoint at half their distance.
Consequently each component is a singleton and |P|=k. This proves (2).

Notice what is NOT claimed: a midpoint component need not equal all
the lattice points in its convex hull. The argument needs only its
hyperedge connectivity and the parity-to-component map. The archived
rank-three counterexamples to component lattice completeness are
fully consistent with this proof.

Finally, under equal budgets, the pairwise null-overlap partition gives

    M=mu(union_i H_i)=sum_i mu(H_i)=rD.

Combining this exact identity with the cap count proves (3).

## 5. Sharpness of the cap-count constant

For every n>=0 and d>=1 take

    C=[0,1]^n times K,

where K is any full-dimensional centrally symmetric convex body in
R^d with center zero and volume V. Then P={0,1}^n, k=c(P)=2^n.
Fix a nonzero continuous direction u. For each binary vertex b let

    ell_b(z)=sum_{j:b_j=0} z_j+sum_{j:b_j=1}(1-z_j).

It is zero at b and at least one at every other integer base of C.
Choose L>max_{x in K}|u.x| and define two caps per b by

    H_(b,+)={u.x-L ell_b(z)>=0},
    H_(b,-)={-u.x-L ell_b(z)>=0}.

Each cap is empty on every other integer fiber. On its own fiber
the pair gives opposite through-center cuts, each of volume V/2.
The family is a partition up to null overlaps, no cap captures an
entire positive fiber, and all its budgets equal D=V/2. It has

    r=2^(n+1)=2k,       M=2^n V,       D=M/(2k).

This verifies sharpness of (1) and (3) for the stated partition class,
including n=0. The caps use finite integer coefficients and retain
the original lattice.

## 6. Limits of the result

Equal budgets by themselves do not imply disjoint traces. Even one
triangle has three canonical centroid caps, each of area 4/9 of the
triangle, which cover the triangle and have positive-area overlaps.
Taking the product with an integer interval preserves actual midpoint
inclusions and these overlapping equal-budget cap covers. Thus no
step in the proof licenses applying the partition incidence conclusion
to an arbitrary critical-cap cover.

If a cap captures an entire positive fiber, the interior two-cut mark
used in Section 3 is unavailable on that fiber. The present proof does
not remove or charge such fibers. The separate theorem
`candidate 05b459fea3722ebb`
proves the weaker r<=2k bound even with full-fiber ownership, by a
projection-Helly argument, and gives an exact four-cap example showing
that r<=2c(P) and (2) are then false. That theorem also covers constant
positive fractional incidence on each fiber. Neither theorem treats
arbitrary positive fractional covers with nonconstant multiplicity.

The useful exact conclusion is therefore a structural dichotomy in the
specified budget range: a sufficiently small equal-budget cover under
the no-whole-fiber premise cannot be a partition; it must have genuine
positive measured overlap. Quantifying that overlap in a way that
supplies the sharp general OC constant remains a separate problem.
